summary:
Choosing a crop rotation means balancing drought risk, soil health, planting windows and markets, but the data needed is scattered and what suits one farm may not suit another. Sowlaris brings it together in one tool, using NASA Earth observation data.

For a farm in Riley County, Kansas, Sowlaris runs a daily soil-water model driven by NASA POWER weather and GPM IMERG rainfall for 2005–2025. It uses USDA soil data, including a clay-rich layer that limits how much water the root zone can store. Each rotation is scored on water, climate fit, soil health, erosion protection, pest break and market potential, after removing rotations the farm can’t actually carry out.

Sowlaris combines NASA-driven crop-water estimates, farm-specific soil limits, feasibility checks, adjustable priorities and visible trade-offs in one explainable workflow. It reports its own limits openly. It flags close calls instead of hiding them. It compares its water model with ECOSTRESS satellite data and reports the disagreement.

With default priorities, the top suggestion is corn (then a cereal rye cover crop) → soybean → winter wheat (then hairy vetch). It scores 0.78, against 0.70 for the farm’s current corn–soybean rotation.
details:
The Problem

Farmers choosing a crop rotation must weigh drought risk, soil health, planting schedules and market opportunities. The data needed is spread across many sources, and the best rotation for one farm may be wrong for the next.

What Sowlaris does

Sowlaris turns NASA Earth observations and USDA farm records into a rotation plan in plain language. The farmer sets their priorities and answers four practical questions:

  • Is irrigation available?
  • Should the recommended rotation require no more crop water than the current rotation?
  • Can a cover crop be planted before harvest?
  • Is there livestock or a forage market?

Sowlaris then compares the current rotation with the best feasible alternatives. Each option shows its strongest and weakest point, what changes compared with today, and a status: feasible, conditional or infeasible.

How it Works

Water

A daily FAO-56 soil-water model is driven by NASA POWER weather and GPM IMERG precipitation (2005–2025). From USDA SSURGO soil data, the model infers a clay-rich layer and estimates about 109 mm of plant-available water in the corn root zone. This is a model assumption based on soil data, not a field measurement.

Yield risk

Water stress is converted into modelled relative yield-loss estimates using FAO-33 yield response factors. The model identifies severe water stress in the 2012 drought. Comparisons with historical yields also show that it underestimates how large extreme-drought losses can be.

Scoring

Each rotation is scored on six criteria: water, climate fit, soil health, erosion protection, pest break and market potential. Rotations the farm can’t carry out, such as a cover crop with no time to plant it, are removed before ranking. When two options score within 0.02 of each other, the app calls it a close call.

Validation and honesty

ECOSTRESS check. The modelled ratio of actual to reference evapotranspiration (ETa/ET0) is about 0.71, compared with about 0.53 from ECOSTRESS. We report this as an unresolved validation limitation.

Sensitivity

Under the default priorities, the same top two rotations remained in 79% of 300 sensitivity runs that varied uncertain model parameters. Under market-focused priorities, the same top-two pair remained in only 42% of runs, showing greater sensitivity to uncertain parameters.

Random Forest yield model

Leave-one-year-out mean absolute error was 11.2 percentage points of normal yield, compared with 15.4 for a simple baseline. Preprocessing was done within each training fold to prevent data leakage. The model is used only as a diagnostic and never changes the ranking.

Known limitations are listed inside the app.

NASA Data

  • Direct inputs to the recommendation: NASA POWER weather data and GPM IMERG precipitation provide the direct climate inputs for the recommendation model.
  • Supporting observations and checks: SMAP soil moisture (an independent soil-moisture check), ECOSTRESS evapotranspiration and land surface temperature (model validation), MODIS NDVI/EVI (vegetation context) and SRTM elevation (site context). All four were retrieved through NASA AppEEARS.
  • Other sources: USDA CropScape, SSURGO, NASS county yields and FAO GAEZ v4.

Tools

Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn) and Streamlit. 162 automated tests cover units, missing data, drought behaviour, feasibility rules, reproducibility and the app.

What is new

Sowlaris combines in one explainable workflow:

  • NASA-driven daily crop-water calculations
  • farm-specific soil limits
  • feasibility checks before ranking
  • farmer-adjustable priorities
  • transparent trade-offs with sensitivity testing

Intended impact

Sowlaris aims to help farmers explore drought-aware rotations, understand the trade-offs, and identify options worth discussing with local agricultural advisers before planting. It currently covers one Kansas study site. It could expand to other regions once the models are calibrated and validated there.

Use of AI

We used AI assistants, including Claude and ChatGPT, to support coding, debugging, testing, documentation and technical review. The team selected the scientific methods, evaluated the outputs and takes responsibility for the submitted work.
